learning_goal: Name the three heads of pectoralis major and their origins, say where all three insert and why the tendon is folded, and give the movement each head produces.

structures.name: clavicular part of right pectoralis major
structures.label: Pectoralis major — clavicular head
structures.narration: From the front of the medial half of the clavicle. Its fibres run downward and laterally, so this head flexes the arm at the shoulder.

structures.name: sternocostal part of right pectoralis major
structures.label: Pectoralis major — sternocostal head
structures.narration: The bulk of the muscle. It arises from the front of the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages, and its fibres run almost straight laterally. This is the head that adducts and medially rotates.

structures.name: abdominal part of right pectoralis major
structures.label: Pectoralis major — abdominal head
structures.narration: A small slip from the aponeurosis of external oblique over the upper rectus sheath. Its fibres run upward and laterally, and they end up highest of all on the humerus.

structures.name: right clavicle
structures.label: Clavicle
structures.narration: The medial half gives origin to the clavicular head. Deltoid takes the lateral third, and the gap between the two is the deltopectoral groove.

structures.name: manubrium
structures.label: Manubrium
structures.narration: The upper part of the sternal origin.

structures.name: body of sternum
structures.label: Body of sternum
structures.narration: The sternocostal head grips the front of the sternum down to about the sixth cartilage. The two muscles meet at the midline but do not cross it.

structures.name: right second costal cartilage
structures.label: 2nd costal cartilage
structures.narration: The costal cartilages, not the ribs, are what the muscle arises from.

structures.name: right third costal cartilage
structures.label: 3rd costal cartilage
structures.narration: Origin continues down the cartilages in order.

structures.name: right fourth costal cartilage
structures.label: 4th costal cartilage
structures.narration: The fourth space is the level of the nipple in a man, and a useful landmark on this wall.

structures.name: right fifth costal cartilage
structures.label: 5th costal cartilage
structures.narration: Origin continues.

structures.name: right sixth costal cartilage
structures.label: 6th costal cartilage
structures.narration: The lowest cartilage of the sternocostal origin. Below this the abdominal slip takes over.

structures.name: right external oblique
structures.label: External oblique — aponeurosis
structures.narration: The abdominal head arises from this sheet, which is why pectoralis major is continuous with the abdominal wall and not just a chest muscle.

structures.name: right rectus abdominis
structures.label: Rectus abdominis
structures.narration: The sheath in front of this muscle is what the abdominal slip lies on.

structures.name: right humerus
structures.label: Humerus
structures.narration: The humerus. Pectoralis major reaches it in one place only, high on the front of the shaft.

structures.label: Bicipital groove
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT within the proximal quarter of the humerus (z:0.72,1) — both heads of pectoralis major reach the lateral lip beside the tubercles there, and restricted to that slab the two agree to 4.1 mm (gaps 0.97 mm, 0.39 mm)
structures.narration: All three heads converge on the lateral lip of the bicipital groove. Remember the three muscles of the groove: pectoralis major on the lateral lip, teres major on the medial lip, latissimus dorsi on the floor.
structures.reviewed_note: opened in the 3D viewer and looked at: the patch lands on the feature the label names. Checked by Claude on 2026-08-28 at Frank’s request, not by an independent human reader — the measurement and its evidence are in calibrated_by.

structures.name: right pectoralis minor
structures.label: Pectoralis minor
structures.narration: Directly deep to pectoralis major, from ribs three to five up to the coracoid process. It is the landmark that divides the axillary artery into its three parts.

structures.name: right subclavius
structures.label: Subclavius
structures.narration: A small muscle under the clavicle. With pectoralis minor it is enclosed by the clavipectoral fascia.

structures.name: right serratus anterior
structures.label: Serratus anterior
structures.narration: It clothes the side of the chest wall deeper again, running back to the medial border of the scapula.

structures.name: clavicular part of right deltoid
structures.label: Deltoid — clavicular fibres
structures.narration: The other side of the deltopectoral groove. Both muscles reach the clavicle, and the gap between them is where the cephalic vein climbs to reach the axillary vein.

structures.name: right latissimus dorsi
structures.label: Latissimus dorsi
structures.narration: The muscle that forms the posterior axillary fold, and the antagonist that shares two of pectoralis major's actions — adduction and medial rotation — from behind.

views.title: The muscle of the front of the chest
views.narration: Pectoralis major is a thick fan covering the upper chest wall. It has a wide origin along the midline and a narrow insertion on the humerus, which is what a muscle looks like when it is built to pull the arm towards the body. Its lower border makes the anterior axillary fold you can pinch between your fingers.

views.title: Three heads, three origins
views.narration: Read the origin from the top down. Clavicular head from the medial half of the clavicle. Sternocostal head from the front of the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages. Abdominal head from the aponeurosis of external oblique. The heads are named for what they come from, so the name is the answer.

views.title: The tendon folds on itself
views.narration: All three heads end on the lateral lip of the bicipital groove, but not in the order you expect. The clavicular fibres go in front and reach lowest. The sternocostal and abdominal fibres fold behind them and reach highest. So the tendon has two laminae and the lowest fibres of the muscle insert highest on the bone. That twist is why the muscle can pull the arm through such a wide arc without slackening.

views.title: What each head does
views.narration: The whole muscle adducts and medially rotates the arm. Split it and the two halves oppose each other. The clavicular head flexes the shoulder, so it lifts the arm forward from the side. The sternocostal head extends the flexed arm, so it pulls the arm back down again. Test the clavicular head by pushing the arm forward against resistance and the sternocostal head by pressing the hands together in front of the chest. With the arm fixed above the head, both heads pull the trunk up to the arm, which is how you climb.

views.title: The deltopectoral groove
views.narration: Between the clavicular head and deltoid is a furrow, the deltopectoral groove. The cephalic vein runs up in it and dives through the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein. At the top the groove widens into the deltopectoral triangle, bounded by clavicle, deltoid and pectoralis major, and that triangle is the surface landmark used for infraclavicular blocks and for shoulder approaches. Look for the groove itself between the two muscles on screen: the vein and the fascia are being described, not shown, because neither exists as a model here.

views.title: Cut across the chest wall
views.narration: Cut across at the level of the fourth cartilage and count inward. Skin and superficial fascia, and in a woman the breast lies in that layer. Then pectoral fascia, then pectoralis major. Then the clavipectoral fascia with pectoralis minor inside it. Then the ribs and intercostals, then pleura. The breast sits on the fascia over the muscle, which is why a carcinoma tethered to the muscle becomes fixed when the arm is abducted against resistance.

views.title: Nerve supply and clinical points
views.narration: Nothing in this beat is drawn — there is no nerve and no vessel in this model set, so hold the heads on screen and put the supply onto them from the words. Both pectoral nerves supply this muscle: the lateral pectoral nerve from the lateral cord to the clavicular head, the medial pectoral nerve from the medial cord to the sternocostal and abdominal heads. The medial nerve pierces pectoralis minor on its way, so the nerve named medial lies lateral to the other one at the muscle. Three things to carry: absence of the sternocostal head is the defining feature of Poland syndrome; the muscle is a workhorse flap for head, neck and chest wall reconstruction because its blood supply from the thoracoacromial artery enters near the clavicle; and a rupture at the tendon tears the sternocostal head, typically in bench pressing, leaving a lump on the chest and a hollow at the axillary fold.

gaps: No pectoral nerves and no thoracoacromial artery. Every nerve and vessel in this scene is narrated over muscle and bone: the lateral and medial pectoral nerves, the cephalic vein in the deltopectoral groove, and the arterial supply that makes the muscle a flap. The catalog holds two optic nerves and no named branch of the axillary artery, so beats 5 and 7 describe structures the student cannot see.

No fascia. The pectoral fascia and the clavipectoral fascia are both taught here — the clavipectoral fascia is what the cephalic vein pierces and what encloses pectoralis minor and subclavius — and neither has a model. The cross-section beat counts layers by narration.

No breast. Searching the catalog for breast, mammary gland or nipple returns nothing at all. The relationship of the breast to the pectoral fascia is narrated in beat 6, but the curriculum's separate 'Breast (mammary gland)' entry cannot be authored as a 3D scene from this catalog, and is authored in diagram mode for exactly that reason.

The intercostal muscles exist only as three unsided whole-body meshes (external, internal, innermost), so they are named in the cross-section narration rather than shown; adding one would render the entire rib cage's worth of muscle on both sides.

There is no separate mesh for the bicipital groove or its lips, so the insertion is carried by a measured landmark anchor on the humerus rather than by geometry of its own. The anchor was derived as a contact point, restricted to the proximal quarter of the shaft, from both heads of pectoralis major; the two witnesses agree to 4.1 mm. The lateral lip is therefore marked on the bone, but the medial lip and the floor of the groove — named in the same beat for teres major and latissimus dorsi — are not.
